headline: Adopted consent agenda covering BPD and BFD reports and appeal hearing scheduling amendment, unanimously.
summary: The committee heard public comments for and against the Burlington Forward resolution, then adopted a consent agenda covering BPD and BFD reports and a proposed amendment to BCO Sec 41-45A(f)(3). The committee also received presentations on library public safety data, a City Circle update, and discussed the latest draft of the Burlington Forward resolution, taking no action on these items.
decisions: Adopted the consent agenda, including the BPD report, BFD report, and proposed amendment to BCO Sec 41-45A(f)(3) on appeal hearing scheduling timeline.

Page 1 of 4 
 
 
Public Safety Committee 
Thursday, August 27, 2026 
Remote via Zoom/In-Person in Sharon Bushor Conference Room, 1st Floor, City Hall, 
Burlington, Vermont   
DRAFT MINUTES 
  
Members Present:  Buddy Singh (Chair), Melo Grant, Evan Litwin, Laura Sanchez-Parkinson 
  
Staff Present: Jessica Brown (City Attorney), Rachel Jolly (CEDO Assistant Director), Becky 
Penberthy (CCCJC Justice Programs Manager), Mary Danko (Library Director), David Lines 
(Howard Center Street Outreach at FFL) 
 
Public Present: Maddie Posen, Bella Fearn, Brian Clifford, Tammie Brownell, Chris McGrath, 
Jonathan Farrell, Ed Baker, Nolan Rampy 
 
Meeting called to order at 5:32 PM by Councilor Singh. 
  
1.   Adopt the Agenda 
     1.01 Adopt the Agenda 
  
Motion to Adopt Agenda as written.   
 
Motion by Councilor Litwin, Seconded by Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson 
Final Resolution: Motion Passes 
Yes: Unanimous 
 
2.    Adopt Minutes 
      2.01 Motion to adopt draft minutes from July 23, 2026 and July 27, 2026 
 
Motion to adopt draft minutes from July 23, 2026 and July 27, 2026 as written. 
 
Motion by Councilor Litwin, Seconded by Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson 
Final Resolution: Motion Passes 
Yes: Unanimous 
 
3.    Public Forum 
      3.01 Verbal Comments 
 
Maddie Posen of Ward 8 expressed support for the Burlington Forward framework and 
commended City Council members for passing the resolution asking for help from the governor 
and implores the governor, mayor, and council to come together to solve these problems, 
including enforcing existing laws against drug use as part of that effort and addressing public 
safety concerns in the downtown area.  
 
Bella Fearn, of Ward 3 and an organizer for Vermont Harm Reduction Advocates, provided 
notes to the Committee on proposed changes to the Burlington Forward resolution and spoke to
Page 2 of 4 
 
 
Section 4.03 regarding the overdose prevention center, stating that the resolution as written 
would create more barriers to establishing OPC and restrictions increase risk of overdose and 
creates barriers to alternatives for public substance use, worsening the issue of public drug use.  
Fearn recommended that councilors look at the Service Assessment Report completed in March 
2026 to inform Burlington Forward as far as the framework relates to the Overdose Prevention 
Center and how to ensure it would be accessible for those in need of its services and ultimately 
ensure the center’s effectiveness.  Fearn also added Vermonters for Criminal Justice Reform is 
starting an NPA tour to provide updates and education about the OPC to community members, 
with the next meeting being September 9 for Ward 1 at 7:30 PM.   
 
Brian Clifford, who organizes with mutual aid groups operating in City Hall Park and works with 
BTV Cop Watch, expressed opposition to the law enforcement-related measures of Burlington 
Forward, stating more police presence downtown will not have the desired impact, citing that the 
last few summers of increased police patrols have not resulted in a drop in drug-related activity 
in the downtown.  Clifford also noted concerns about racial disparities and Use of Force 
incidents only worsening with more police presence and that councilors need to consider how 
black neighbors will be impacted by policies from Burlington Forward.   
 
Tammie Brownell, a Burlington resident and business owner, commented we need to expand our 
definition of safety beyond physical safety and think about the general public’s mental health.  
Brownell emphasized supporting businesses and strengthening the overall community will allow 
Burlington to be in a better position to support the unhoused population, and that consequences 
pave the way to recovery.   
 
Chris McGrath, a Burlington resident, expressed concern that the Burlington Forward 
resolution’s call for more law enforcement presence and activity will lead to short-term success 
but not yield long-term meaningful results, stating that history has shown us this does not work.   
 
Jonathan Farrell, Ward 4 resident and executive director of COTS, expressed support for the 
Burlington Forward resolution because it will bring people together to talk about strategies for 
downtown and guiding people to recovery and believes the current situation is detrimental to 
everyone and enforcement of existing laws is important.   
 
Ed Baker, speaking as someone with lived experience of substance use disorder, commented the 
most unsafe population are the ones dying from overdose on the streets, stating they have been 
alienated from society and struggle with many issues and trauma beyond houselessness and 
addiction.  Baker states those factors make this small population difficult to engage, which is the 
main benefit of the overdose prevention center because it would meet these people where they 
are at, noting that it is a small but necessary part of the overall long-term solution the community 
needs, and to obstruct it is to worsen the problem everyone is trying to solve.   
 
Nolan Rampy, a Howard Center clinician and president of the Howard Center Union, echoed 
Baker’s comments and stated being against the Burlington Forward resolution.  Rampy shared 
they have witnessed funding for social services go down year after year, and that the resolution 
only offers a solution in terms of more punitive action against a vulnerable population to make 
downtown Burlington safe for commerce, which is not the way to do it.  Rampy said actions like
Page 3 of 4 
 
 
rezoning so Food Not Cops cannot serve food to the homeless community or prevent needle 
exchange programs is gross, and while the problem desperately needs to be addressed, this 
resolution is only going to bring law enforcement down on the most vulnerable population.  
 
Public Forum closed at 6:05 PM.  
 
4.   Consent Agenda 
     4.01  BPD Report with questions/answers from committee members 
 
Adopted as part of the consent agenda. 
 
     4.02  BFD Report with questions/answers from comittee members 
 
Adopted as part of the consent agenda. 
 
     4.03  Proposed Amendment to BCO Sec 41-45A(f)(3) - Appeal Hearing Scheduling 
Timeline 
 
Adopted as part of the consent agenda. 
 
Motion to adopt the consent agenda as written.   
 
Motion by Councilor Litwin, Seconded by Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson 
Final Resolution: Motion Passes 
Yes: Unanimous 
 
Discussion:  
Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson commented their disappointment at chiefs’ absence and stated the 
Committee would have benefited from the chiefs’ presence at this meeting.  Councilor Grant 
seconded.   
 
5.  Deliberative Agenda 
     5.01 Mary Danko Fletcher Free Library Public Safety Data/Feedback Report 
 
Library Director Mary Danko with David Lines from Howard Center Street Outreach gave a 
presentation on Fletcher Free Library’s experiences and approach to public safety in the last 
year.  No action was taken.   
 
     5.02 Rachel Jolly CJC: Update on City Circle  
 
CCCJC Director Rachel Jolly and Justice Programs Manager Becky Penberthy provided an 
update on City Circle to the Committee.  No action was taken.   
 
     5.03 Discussions on Items in Burlington Forward
Page 4 of 4 
 
 
The Committee discussed the latest recirculated draft of the Burlington Forward resolution and 
how they will approach work sessions.  No action taken.   
 
6.  Adjournment 
     6.01 Motion to Adjourn 
 
The meeting was adjourned at 8:07 PM.
